title: It’s the Paperwork, Not the Work, Causing Enrollees To Lose Medicaid in Nebraska
summary: Data from the months after the state’s early rollout of new federal work requirements bolsters concerns that red tape will leave many stuck without coverage.
content: When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Donald Trump’s sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches. Many also watched the Cornhusker State’s experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027. On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready. They’ll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don’t meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don’t comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren’t working. Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory. “The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans’ chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans,” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement . Democrats’ massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they’ll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they’re fully enforced. The Basics Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states , along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show , so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states. But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034. The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called “medically frail.” It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska. On May 1, Nebraska became the first state to implement the work requirements. After it began dropping people from coverage in August, 7% of Nebraska Medicaid enrollees who were subject to the requirements when renewing their coverage, or 533 adults, were disenrolled because of the new rules, according to the latest state data . Nebraska’s Medicaid agency was able to verify that 8 in 10 enrollees met the new rules using various state and federal databases. Those people didn’t have to deal with requests for more information, interim state Medicaid director Jeremy Brunssen told KFF Health News. About 14% of new Medicaid applicants subject to the new rules, or 557 people, had been denied because of the work requirements since they were implemented. But the state data also shows some troubling issues. For example, 92% of cases in which existing enrollees lost coverage were due to procedural or paperwork issues rather than state determinations that they did not meet the new work rules. Brunssen attributes that high percentage to the state having to verify the numerous ways people can meet the new requirements or exemptions. “It’s not as simple as typical eligibility enrollment that you can meet via income and household size,” he said. Many enrollees lost coverage because they did not respond to the state’s outreach. Those enrollees may have deemed themselves ineligible or were unsure how to respond, Brunssen said. The rate of procedural denials is much higher than in prior years, according to data analyzed by KFF . Critics fear it means people who may still qualify are losing coverage. “This is definitely a red-flag warning,” said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska, a trade group representing federally funded community health centers. “The high proportion of procedural denials is troubling.” Navigating the New Requirements Cheri Stollar, 48, of Lincoln, Nebraska, received her Medicaid renewal notice in the mail in early November and was confused about which documents to submit to the state to prove she works as a mental health therapist. She also didn’t understand why she had less than a week to respond. She said she tried to call the state Medicaid agency but could not get through. Her renewal has since been completed. “I want to make sure I send in everything they need,” said Stollar, who lives in a three-bedroom mobile home with three of her four children. She has been on Medicaid for two years and credits the coverage for enabling her to afford medications for depression, sleep, and an ulcer. She said the new law will make it harder for people like her to get and stay covered, which will make it harder to stay healthy — and get and keep a job. Behnke said enrollees calling the state Medicaid agency for help have been put on hold for up to two hours. The assistance line operates only on weekdays, during daytime hours, making it difficult for people who work to call. State Medicaid officials say they are working to add more staff to reduce wait times. One challenge in evaluating Nebraska’s implementation is that the state, as of mid-November, had released data only through August. State officials said this summer that they would post an online dashboard with various performance metrics to improve public transparency. That hasn’t happened yet. “We have seen a lot of negative effects so far,” said Sarah Maresh, program director at Nebraska Appleseed, a nonprofit social justice advocacy group. “Every person that goes without coverage is a problem.” She worries that people are being deterred from applying to Medicaid because of the policy. Brunssen, the interim Medicaid director, defended his state’s performance. “We are experiencing what we expected,” he said in an October interview at a National Association of Medicaid Directors conference in Maryland. “The vast majority of people newly applying, or for those going through redetermination, are getting coverage or retaining coverage.” Yet, Brunssen noted, it’s still early. Fewer than 25% of Medicaid enrollees subject to the work requirement have had to prove they meet the new rules to retain coverage. The rest won’t be completed until next summer, he said. The state’s Department of Health and Human Services, which operates its Medicaid program, has used various methods to inform enrollees about the new rules, such as letters, emails, texts, and messages in an online portal, Brunssen said. “Most Medicaid enrollees know about the new rules,” he said, attributing awareness to community partners and managed-care companies that helped get the word out. “I feel like we’ve done everything in our power to communicate what was coming,” he said. Brunssen noted the state has taken advantage of a federal option to let enrollees self-attest that they meet exemptions. All declarations must be truthful, or enrollees could face perjury charges. Self-attestation is as easy as checking a box on an online form. No supporting documents are required. That’s made it easier for people to comply, Brunssen said. The state has also exempted people living in three counties with high unemployment rates and in two counties declared federal disaster areas because of weather events, he said. “Our goal is to make sure people who are eligible get or retain coverage,” Brunssen said. Some enrollees say the state could do more to make the process easier. Chalandria James, 37, of Omaha, was worried about whether she still had Medicaid coverage after she tried to renew in July but did not hear back from the state, despite repeated calls. Unsure of her coverage status, she canceled a doctor’s appointment to check her blood pressure. It took until September, and a multi-hour visit to the state agency office, for her to find out she still had Medicaid and was exempt from the work requirement because she had a child under 14. “It was nerve-racking not knowing,” said James, a community health worker and doula. In Nebraska, about 37% of enrollees met the work requirement while 61% qualified for an exemption — with the most common reasons being medical frailty or caregiving. Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University’s Center for Children and Families, said Nebraska’s experience shows the work rules do little to promote work, since most who can are already working. “This policy punishes low-income people by subjecting them to serious, often insurmountable, hurdles,” she said. Even with data showing the large majority of enrollees working or meeting an exemption, Brunssen said the new requirements still are a good idea. “Part of being a good, healthy person does involve engagement with the community,” he said, “and we think there is value in the work we are doing in this space.” Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? title: Sticker Shock Looms as a Major Challenge in Push for Single-Payer Healthcare
summary: Any discussion of a universal health plan in the U.S. always comes with concerns about massive costs. The challenge for proponents is to explain to voters that Americans already spend more than $5 trillion on healthcare each year.
content: As an Oregon panel finalized its proposal for statewide universal healthcare this month, opposition had already coalesced around a familiar theme: The costs and the new taxes needed to support it will be staggeringly large. The panel’s estimates place the cost of the plan at $69.7 billion a year starting in 2032. The same arguments are being made on the national level about “Medicare for All,” which gained renewed life after Democrats’ victorious blue wave in the midterms. One recent White House cost estimate pegged the annual price tag at $4.7 trillion. But single-payer proponents, researchers, and academics are countering the perceived sticker shock with another stark reality: If you think universal healthcare would be expensive, you should see what we pay now. “We already do spend trillions of dollars on healthcare,” said Cynthia Cox , a senior vice president at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. “It’s just that it’s not only spent by the federal government but also by states, individuals, private insurers, and other third-party payers.” Increased government spending under a universal health plan would replace much, if not all, of what is currently being paid by companies and consumers, while extending health coverage to more people, its proponents argue. And they say many people would end up paying less for a universal health plan’s taxes than consumers now shell out in premiums and other out-of-pocket costs. But those nuances represent some of the biggest challenges of selling a universal healthcare system to the public. Unless backers can figure out the messaging to alleviate fears of massive new taxes and government spending, current efforts to implement a single-payer, universal healthcare plan could be doomed to the same fate as previous efforts in places such as California, Massachusetts, and Vermont. Educating the Public In 2014, then-Vermont Gov. Peter Shumlin , a Democrat, pulled the plug on the state’s single-payer push. Difficulties in implementing the state’s healthcare exchange under the Affordable Care Act had sapped the political capital he needed to push through the plan’s tax increases, even though the state expected to save money for Vermonters overall. Single-player ballot measures in California, Massachusetts, and Oregon also struggled to garner even a quarter of the voting public’s support. The Democratic wave in this year’s midterm elections, however, ushered in a number of Medicare-for-All proponents, most notably Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who campaigned on a universal healthcare platform. The change in congressional control is also expected to elevate Sen. Bernie Sanders , a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats and is the best-known advocate for Medicare for All, to chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. That is likely to push a debate over single-payer healthcare — and its costs or savings — to the forefront in the next two years, leading into the 2028 presidential election. “Most people think that what they pay out-of-pocket or out of their paycheck directly is what it costs, and they’re not as familiar with the larger piece,” said John McDonough , a health policy professor at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. “Nobody on Medicare knows what that costs. Nobody on Medicaid knows what it costs. Very few people on the exchanges know. So, with something brand-new, it’s a massive education effort just to get to the starting line.” The White House Council of Economic Advisers, for example, estimated in October that a plan to extend Medicare benefits to all Americans would cost the federal government $47 trillion over 10 years. And a recent Wall Street Journal op-ed from Joel Zinberg of the conservative-leaning Paragon Health Institute decried that figure as a massive increase in federal spending. But the latest government data shows total spending for healthcare from all sources in the U.S. reached about $5.3 trillion in 2024. And that spending is on pace to top $72 trillion combined over the 10-year period from 2025 through 2034. While that estimate includes spending for the military and veterans, the Indian Health Service, and elective services that might not be covered under a universal health plan, the price tag for national healthcare coverage still could look like a bargain. “People are aware that healthcare is very expensive and that they have trouble getting access to it even if they have decent insurance,” said Stephanie Woolhandler , a public health professor at the City University of New York’s Hunter College. “But if they think $47 trillion is a big number relative to what we’re spending now, they’re mistaken.” Oregon Shares Same Challenge The Oregon Universal Health Plan Governance Board released its report to the state legislature on Nov. 23. The report outlines a plan to create a public corporation that would rely on corporate and personal taxes to fund a statewide healthcare system, providing care to nearly everyone in the state, with no premiums, copays, or other deductibles. The legislature could vote on the plan as early as next year or refer the proposal to voters as a ballot measure in 2028. Critics are focused on the total cost of the proposal. Oregon Senate Republican Leader Bruce Starr said in a news release that the plan would increase the entire state budget by 43%, with “unfathomable” new taxes coming out of the pockets of Oregonians. “Handing control of hospitals, doctors, and insurance to the same bureaucracy that has failed at basic responsibilities, and layering on double digit payroll and income taxes, is irresponsible and fiscally unsound,” he said. At their Oct. 15 meeting, members of the Universal Health Plan Governance Board bristled at characterizations of their plan as a massive cost increase to state taxpayers. Their analyses show that up to 3 out of every 5 people would pay less under a single-payer system. An analysis commissioned for the state from the Milliman consulting firm found that without changes, total spending on healthcare per year in Oregon would reach at least $76.3 billion by 2032. The board estimated that a universal health plan would cost about $69.7 billion that year, not including one-time start-up or transition costs. “I just don’t want people to — because I’ve seen they’ve already started to — make all kinds of assertions about our work and saying, ‘It’s unaffordable, we can’t do it, end of story,’” Mike Leahy, a former health plan executive who serves on the Oregon board, said during an October meeting. “I’d like us to give this plan a chance of happening.” The board maintains that the plan would save money compared with the status quo by reducing administrative costs, negotiating drug prices, and combating fraud, waste, and abuse while allowing the state to cover all Oregonians with a rich set of benefits. Oregon’s design, like Vermont’s, is modeled after the national health system of Taiwan, which is frequently pointed to as a high-performing system, with public satisfaction rates topping 90%. Taiwan’s program, implemented 30 years ago, relies on nearly equal shares of contributions from households, companies, and the government to pay for services. Debate Moves Front and Center Democratic leaders in Washington, D.C., have already indicated plans for a major push on healthcare affordability in the upcoming Congress. President Donald Trump is seen as unsupportive, if not outright hostile , to the notion of a government-financed, single-payer health system. Backers of universal healthcare say the next two years, as they wait for a potentially more cooperative federal administration, will be crucial for debating how a single-payer system could be designed and financed, and how it could be sold to voters. “What people fail to realize is that we’re already paying the entire bill,” said Deborah Richter, a family physician and board president for the advocacy group Vermont Health Care for All . “So you’re either paying in taxes, Medicare, Medicaid taxes, or you’re paying out-of-pocket for copays and deductibles, or coinsurance. You’re paying increased prices and getting lower wages.” But much of those costs are hidden from consumers, she said, and universal healthcare proposals bring all that spending together into a single number, front and center. “People get the impression that this is on top of what they’re already paying,” Richter said. “And they’re already saying: ‘Oh, my God. I’m paying this. I can’t pay this extra tax.’” KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. title: Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
summary: Medicare’s zero-premium drug plans are disappearing, millions are losing their plans, and the average prescription drug plan premium could rise 50% if you stay put. Here’s what to check.
content: Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people . The coverage choices are complex and often consequential. Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn’t one plan. It’s more like a build-your-own-insurance menu. Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there’s no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn’t cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services. As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D , the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums. “People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs,” said David Lipschutz , a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy. The Hassle Saves Money Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It’s a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can’t find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn’t tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs. Some beneficiaries who didn’t have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt to spread out over the course of the year. Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don’t shop around could be leaving money on the table. “It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027,” she said. Some Plans No Longer Offered An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they’ll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it’s important to read the fine print and add up the other costs. “There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide,” Lipschutz said. So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover? And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027. “Look at that dollar value specifically,” she said. For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won’t come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life. When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don’t pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage. If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions . Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven’t been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March. F or Shopping Help, Think ‘ SHIP’ Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor’s office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan. For unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free plan counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment , email info@shiphelp.org , or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675. A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help . Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.
